nameStory: The name 'creeping cinquefoil' tells you exactly how this plant grows and what to look for! 'Creeping' describes its low, sprawling habit as it sends out long runners across the ground, while 'cinquefoil' comes from the French 'cinq' (five) and 'feuille' (leaf), referring to its distinctive five-leaflet leaves. Think of it as the plant that creeps along counting to five!
description: Creeping cinquefoil is a low-growing perennial that spreads by sending out long, trailing stems called runners, much like a strawberry plant. It forms mats of distinctive hand-shaped leaves, each divided into five toothed leaflets that radiate from a central point like fingers on a hand. The plant produces cheerful yellow flowers with five rounded petals throughout the growing season, and typically stays close to the ground, rarely rising more than a few inches high.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctive hand-shaped leaves with exactly five leaflets radiating from a central point like fingers, each leaflet toothed along the edges and soft to the touch

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with five rounded petals that feel papery when touched, blooming singly on long stalks above the leaves

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Spreads by long, trailing runners that root at nodes, creating expanding mats along the ground rather than growing upright

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Runners are smooth, reddish, and can stretch several feet, rooting wherever they touch moist soil and creating new plants

habitat: Creeping cinquefoil thrives in disturbed soils, roadsides, lawns, and waste areas throughout New England, preferring sunny to partially shaded locations. It's particularly fond of moist, fertile soils but can tolerate a range of conditions from sandy to clayey ground. You'll often find it mixed with grasses and other low-growing weeds in areas that see regular foot traffic or mowing.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as distinctive five-fingered clusters, and the first yellow flowers begin appearing in late spring as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering season with bright yellow blooms appearing continuously, while runners actively spread and root to form expanding colonies.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall, and the green foliage may begin to yellow but often remains visible well into the season.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level in harsh winters, but some leaves may persist in protected areas or during mild winters.

funFact: Despite being in the rose family, creeping cinquefoil was historically used as a substitute for strawberry leaves in folk medicine, and its roots were once harvested to make a reddish dye for leather – earning it the alternate name 'creeping tormentil' because of its astringent, mouth-puckering taste!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with wild strawberry, but creeping cinquefoil has five leaflets per leaf while strawberries have only three, and cinquefoil produces yellow flowers instead of white ones. Remember: 'Five fingers, five petals, it's cinquefoil' versus 'Three leaflets, white flowers, it's strawberry.'
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'European cinquefoil' in some references, this plant is now widely naturalized across North America and behaves more like a native species in most New England ecosystems. The term 'tormentil' in one of its alternate names refers to an old medicinal use for treating digestive 'torment,' though this plant is distinct from true tormentil.
compareHints: Among New England's cinquefoils, creeping cinquefoil is unique for its long trailing runners and five-leaflet leaves – most other cinquefoils like common cinquefoil and dwarf cinquefoil have three leaflets and don't spread by runners. Sulphur cinquefoil grows upright rather than creeping, while rough cinquefoil is much taller and bushier with a completely different growth form.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sulphur cinquefoil stands out from other New England cinquefoils primarily by its bright yellow flowers and consistently five-fingered leaves.

Among New England's cinquefoils, silvery cinquefoil is the only one with dramatically silver-white fuzzy leaf undersides - dwarf and common cinquefoil have plain green undersides, while rough cinquefoil has much larger, coarsely-toothed leaves.
Among New England's cinquefoils, dwarf cinquefoil is distinguished by its truly prostrate, mat-forming habit with rooting runners.
Common cinquefoil differs from dwarf cinquefoil by its longer, more obvious runners and slightly larger flowers.
Unlike other cinquefoils in its genus which typically have five-part leaves (the name cinquefoil means 'five leaves'), mock strawberry has three-part leaves like true strawberries.
Unlike most other New England cinquefoils which have five leaflets, rough cinquefoil stands out with just three leaflets per leaf.
Lesser mock-strawberry differs from other cinquefoils by having three-part leaves instead of the typical five-part leaves (cinque means five in French).
Unlike its lowland cinquefoil relatives that spread by runners or grow as larger plants, dwarf mountain cinquefoil forms tiny, tight cushions and never leaves the alpine zone.

Intermediate cinquefoil differs from common New England cinquefoils like dwarf cinquefoil by its specific leaflet count and arrangement, and from sulphur cinquefoil by its smaller stature and different leaf texture.
Unlike its inland cinquefoil relatives, coast cinquefoil has adapted specifically to maritime conditions with its more compact, mat-forming growth and thicker, more succulent-like leaves.
